title: HTTP/2 — Multiplexing & Binary Framing
summary: How HTTP/2 fixed HTTP/1.1's connection-blocking problem with binary framing and multiplexed streams — the bridge to HTTP/3.

slides.markdown:
HTTP/2 keeps HTTP's semantics (methods, status codes, headers) but replaces the wire format entirely: instead of plaintext lines, the browser and server exchange small binary **frames** multiplexed over a single TCP connection. The payoff is one connection doing the work that used to need six, with far less overhead.

- Same verbs and headers as HTTP/1.1 — just packaged differently on the wire.
- Solves *application-layer* head-of-line blocking, not transport-layer.
- The direct ancestor of HTTP/3, which swaps TCP for QUIC.

HTTP/1.1 sends requests as plain text, one at a time per connection — a response has to fully arrive before the next request can be answered. Browsers work around this by opening **~6 parallel TCP connections per host**, but that's a patch: each connection still serializes its own requests, and DNS/TLS setup repeats per connection.

This is **head-of-line (HOL) blocking at the application layer**: a slow response blocks everything queued behind it on that connection, even with spare network capacity.

HTTP/2's core structural change is a **binary framing layer** sitting between HTTP semantics and TCP. Every message — headers, body — is chopped into small binary **frames**, each tagged with a **stream ID** and a type (`HEADERS`, `DATA`, `SETTINGS`, ...).

Binary framing is faster to parse than parsing text token-by-token, but the real win is what it enables: frames from different streams can be freely interleaved on the wire and reassembled by stream ID on the other end — the mechanism the next Card covers.

slides.subTitle: Streams over one connection
slides.markdown:
Because every frame carries a stream ID, HTTP/2 can interleave frames from several in-flight requests on **one** TCP connection and reassemble them by ID at the other end.

![Three HTTP/2 streams interleaving frames on one TCP connection](assets/http2-stream-multiplexing.svg)

A large response on stream 1 no longer blocks a small response on stream 3 — its frames simply take turns on the wire instead of monopolizing it.

assets.alt: Three HTTP/2 streams interleaving frames on one TCP connection

slides.subTitle: HPACK
slides.markdown:
Every HTTP request repeats near-identical headers (`user-agent`, cookies) that HTTP/1.1 resends, uncompressed, every time. HTTP/2 fixes this with **HPACK**:

- A **static table** of ~60 common header pairs sent as a single index byte.
- A **dynamic table** both sides build as the connection goes on — a header seen once is referenced by index, not resent.
- Huffman coding compresses the rest.

For header-heavy traffic this cuts real bytes on the wire, not just body compression.

**Server push** let a server proactively send resources (e.g. a CSS file) before the client asked for them, anticipating that a requested HTML page would need them next — avoiding a round trip.

In practice it under-delivered: servers routinely pushed resources the browser **already had cached**, wasting bandwidth, and there was no reliable way for the server to know. Chrome removed support in 2022; most of the industry replaced it with **103 Early Hints**, which tells the browser what to preload without forcing bytes it doesn't want.

HTTP/2 lets a client hint how streams should be scheduled relative to each other — e.g. "the HTML and CSS matter more than this background image" — via a **dependency tree** and **weights** in the `HEADERS` frame.

In practice, prioritization was inconsistently implemented across servers and CDNs, and browsers largely stopped relying on it — Chrome moved to a simpler scheme in 2020. It's worth knowing the mechanism exists, but don't expect it to be load-bearing in a modern stack.

![HTTP/1.1 opening six parallel TCP connections vs HTTP/2 multiplexing everything over one](assets/http2-connections-comparison.svg)

HTTP/1.1 papers over its per-connection blocking with parallel connections — each with its own TCP handshake (and TLS handshake, if HTTPS). HTTP/2 needs only **one** connection per origin, so there's one handshake, one congestion-control state, and one place for the server to reason about priority.

assets.alt: HTTP/1.1 opening six parallel TCP connections vs HTTP/2 multiplexing everything over one

slides.markdown:
| | HTTP/1.1 | HTTP/2 |
|---|---|---|
| Connections per origin | ~6 parallel | 1 |
| Format | Plain text | Binary frames |
| Header repetition | Full headers every request | HPACK-compressed, indexed |
| App-layer HOL blocking | Yes, per connection | No — streams interleave |
| Handshake overhead | Repeated per connection | Once per origin |

**How to decide:** you rarely choose this directly — it's negotiated via ALPN during the TLS handshake — but knowing the trade-offs explains why HTTP/2 is a strict upgrade for HTTP-over-TCP, and why HTTP/3 exists at all (next Topic).

slides.subTitle: HOL blocking isn't fully gone
slides.markdown:
A common misstatement: **"HTTP/2 eliminates head-of-line blocking."** It only eliminates it at the **application layer** — one dropped TCP segment on a single connection still stalls *every* HTTP/2 stream on it, because TCP itself delivers bytes in order. HTTP/2 traded per-request blocking for a single point where *transport-layer* loss blocks everything multiplexed on that connection.

This is exactly the gap **QUIC and HTTP/3** were built to close — see [quic-http3](quic-http3).
